primitives.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Past work has shown that under the BTL model, the widely-used maximum-likelihood estimator (MLE) is minimax-optimal in estimating the item parameters, in terms of the mean squared error.
primitives.assumptions: Under the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, where each item has an unknown quality parameter; pairwise comparisons are independent; every pair is compared k times.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the true parameter vector lies exactly at the boundary of the bounded domain (\|\theta^*\|_\infty \leq B), leading to biased estimates.

layer2.mapping: The MLE maps directly to GSI's Maximum Likelihood Posterior Update, where observed outcomes (win/loss) inform the posterior distribution of team abilities. In GSE, it corresponds to the policy evaluation step using historical match data.
layer2.telemetry: Bias in the posterior mean relative to ground-truth team ratings serves as a key telemetry metric for assessing calibration.

primitives.name: Bias Reduction via Stretching
primitives.verbatim_quote: We then propose a simple modification to the MLE, which "stretches" the bounding box of the maximum-likelihood optimizer by a small constant factor from the underlying ground truth domain.
primitives.assumptions: The ground truth parameter vector lies within a bounded domain of radius B; the stretching factor A is chosen larger than B.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the sample size k is finite and the true parameter is near the original boundary, causing the standard MLE to saturate at the bound.

layer2.mapping: The stretching operation creates a "soft-boundary" prior in GSI's Bayesian framework, preventing extreme posterior estimates. In GSE, it implements risk-aversion in the action-value function, reducing overfitting to noisy transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Reduction in the variance of estimated logits after applying the stretch, measured across multiple Monte Carlo simulations.

primitives.name: Minimax Optimality
primitives.verbatim_quote: We show that this simple modification leads to an improved rate in bias, while maintaining minimax-optimality in the mean squared error.
primitives.assumptions: The parameter space is bounded; the number of comparisons per pair k scales appropriately with the number of items d.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the number of samples approaches the information-theoretic limit, where no estimator can achieve better worst-case MSE.

layer2.mapping: Minimax optimality aligns with GSI's robust prediction principle, ensuring that the worst-case regret of betting strategies is minimized. In GSE, it underpins the development of adversarial RL algorithms that perform well under uncertain dynamics.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical comparison of the worst-case MSE achieved by different estimators across synthetic datasets drawn from the BTL model.

reasoning_traces.think:
The Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) for the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model achieves optimal accuracy (minimax-optimal mean squared error) but suffers from systematic bias when the true parameter vector lies near the boundary of the bounded domain. This bias arises because the MLE saturates at the constraint boundary, introducing a directional error that distorts the relative ordering of items. To address this, we introduce a 'stretching' modification: instead of projecting the unconstrained MLE onto the original box [-B, B]^d, we project it onto a slightly larger box [-A, A]^d where A > B. This stretching operation effectively relaxes the hard constraint, allowing the estimator to explore values beyond the nominal range. Mathematically, the stretched MLE solves max_{\theta: \|\theta\|_\infty \leq A} L(\theta | data), where L is the likelihood. By choosing A appropriately, we ensure that the bias decays at a faster rate (O(1/(d k))) compared to the standard MLE (Ω(1/√(d k))). Crucially, this improvement in bias does not sacrifice accuracy: the mean squared error remains minimax-optimal O(1/k). The key insight is that while the standard MLE trades off bias for variance reduction, the stretched MLE redistributes the estimation error in a way that reduces the systematic offset without inflating the overall variance. This construction demonstrates a clean separation between the objectives of accuracy and fairness in statistical estimation, providing a blueprint for designing estimators that are simultaneously optimal and fair.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Sportsbooks and betting platforms can be modeled as decision-making agents seeking to maximize profit while avoiding public arbitrage. They observe historical matchup data and construct estimators for team strengths. Our primitive reveals that their current MLE-based ratings may systematically misprice favorites and underdogs due to boundary bias. By implementing the stretched MLE, they can reduce this bias, leading to more accurate odds that better reflect true probabilities, thereby improving long-term profitability.
